title: Newton's Laws and Gravity
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Newton's Laws and Gravity Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Newton's three laws of motion describe the relationship between force and motion: balanced and unbalanced forces, gravity as a force, and the effect of mass and force on motion. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 6, Physics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 science worksheets (BC): balanced and unbalanced forces, Newton's first, second and third laws, mass, weight and gravity. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: An unbalanced force changes an object's motion.
key_sub: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's first law: an object stays at rest or keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Newton's second law: a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration, and a bigger mass gives a smaller one.

Newton's third law: forces come in pairs; when you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you just as hard. Gravity is a force that pulls masses toward each other; on Earth it gives objects their weight.

Example

A rocket pushes gas down. What pushes the rocket up?

Forces come in pairs.

Answer: the gas pushes back on the rocket

Example

Two forces of 5 N act on a box in opposite directions. Does it start moving?

Are the forces balanced?

Answer: no, the forces are balanced

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep moving.
  • Thinking action and reaction forces cancel out (they act on different objects).
  • Mixing up mass and weight.

faq.q: Why do you lurch forward when a bus stops suddenly?
faq.a: Inertia: your body keeps moving forward (Newton's first law).

faq.q: Does an astronaut have mass in space?
faq.a: Yes. Mass stays the same; only weight changes with gravity.

items.q: Zoe writes an action force: “A swimmer pushes water backward.” What is the reaction force?
c: The air pushes the wings up.
The water pushes the swimmer forward.
The cannonball pushes the cannon backward (recoil).
The wall pushes the skater away.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: Noah writes an action force: “A car tire pushes back on the road.” What is the reaction force?
c: The boat is pushed backward away from the dock.

The road pushes the car forward.
The air pushes the balloon forward.
items.e: Reaction forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on the other object.

items.q: Ethan asks: when a truck and a small car collide, which one feels the bigger force?
c: Both feel forces of the same size.
A truck feels a bigger force.
A small car feels a bigger force.
items.e: Newton's third law: the forces are equal and opposite.

items.q: Nathan asks: when a bowling ball and a tennis ball collide, which one changes its speed more?
c: A tennis ball, because it has less mass.
They change speed by the same amount.
A bowling ball, because it has more mass.
items.e: Equal forces, but the smaller mass accelerates more.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight acts against drag?
items.e: That force is thrust.

items.q: An airplane has thrust = 50 kN and drag = 80 kN. What happens?
items.e: The bigger force wins: 80 kN is more than 50 kN, so the airplane slows down.

items.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
c: Hot air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside.
The burner pushes it up like a rocket.
items.e: Less dense air rises.

items.q: An airplane has thrust = 130 kN and drag = 230 kN. What happens?
items.e: The bigger force wins: 230 kN is more than 130 kN, so the airplane slows down.

items.q: For an airplane to speed up, which must be true?
c: drag must be greater than thrust
thrust must be greater than drag
weight must be greater than lift
items.e: Unbalanced forces change speed.

items.q: What do the ailerons on the wings control?
c: rolling the plane to bank left or right
items.e: Ailerons move in opposite directions.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight comes from the engines of a jet?
items.e: That force is thrust.

items.q: Why is the air harder to fly in high up in the mountains?
c: The air is thinner, so wings make less lift.
items.e: Fewer air particles push on the wing.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight is made when a wing is tilted up slightly into the air (angle of attack)?
items.e: That force is lift.

items.q: An airplane has lift = 280 kN and weight = 230 kN. What happens?
items.e: The bigger force wins: 280 kN is more than 230 kN, so the airplane climbs.

items.q: An airplane is flying level at a steady speed. What is true about the forces?
items.e: Balanced forces mean no change in motion.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight pushes back against the plane as it moves through the air?
items.e: That force is drag.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight pushes the plane forward, made by the engines or propeller?
items.e: That force is thrust.

items.q: Paper airplane A has wide wings. Paper airplane B has narrow wings. Both have the same mass. Which likely glides further?
c: A, because wide wings make more lift
B, because narrow wings make more lift
items.e: Wing area affects lift.

items.q: Which of the four forces of flight acts against lift?
items.e: That force is weight (gravity).
